title: Sitemap Extractor — get a URL list from any sitemap
description: Give it a domain or a sitemap URL. It finds the sitemap (robots.txt, /sitemap.xml and the other usual paths), follows sitemap index files, and returns every URL the site publishes as structured rows. Tick the status-code option to have each URL probed. This is a sitemap parser, not a web crawler: it reads published sitemap files and checks URL status only — it never reads page content.

startUrls.title: Start URLs
startUrls.description:
One or more domains or URLs.

- A bare domain (`example.com`) makes the extractor discover the sitemap through robots.txt and the usual paths (`/sitemap.xml`, `/sitemap_index.xml`, `/wp-sitemap.xml`, …).
- A sitemap URL (`https://example.com/sitemap.xml`) is used directly as the seed. Sitemap index files are followed automatically.
- A normal page URL behaves like a bare domain: the extractor looks for the sitemap belonging to that site.

maxUrls.title: Max URLs
maxUrls.description:
How many URL rows to return at most. This caps the **output** only — it does not cap how much work the run may do. A single sitemap index can reference thousands of child sitemaps, all of which have to be read before the first URL appears. Use `Max total requests` to bound the work.

With `Check status codes` on, each URL is probed at the target's own polite rate, so runtime grows roughly 0.3 s per URL plus the cost of reading the sitemaps. 200 rows is a couple of minutes; 10,000 rows on one host can take well over half an hour. The run summary marks `truncated: true` when this cap is the reason you did not get every URL.

checkStatusCodes.title: Check status codes
checkStatusCodes.description:
Probe every discovered URL and report its HTTP status code and content type.

Uses `HEAD` first and falls back to `GET` only when the server refuses `HEAD` (`405` / `501`). Only the status is recorded — page bodies are never read or stored. Turn this off to get the URL list without the extra requests; the run is then much faster and much cheaper.

followSitemapIndex.title: Follow sitemap index
followSitemapIndex.description: Recurse into `<sitemapindex>` files and read their child sitemaps. Needed for WordPress (`wp-sitemap.xml` is an index of indexes) and for any site that splits its sitemap by section. Turning it off returns only the top-level sitemap's own URLs.

maxSitemapDepth.title: Max sitemap depth
maxSitemapDepth.description: How deep to recurse through nested sitemap indexes. Depth 1 reads one level of children; depth 3 covers a WordPress install, which is an index of indexes. Cycles (A → B → A) are detected and refused regardless of this setting.

includeSubdomains.title: Include subdomains
includeSubdomains.description:
Keep URLs whose host is a subdomain of the start URL (e.g. `shop.example.com` when you started at `example.com`). Matching uses the Public Suffix List, so `example.co.uk` is treated as one site and `example.co.uk` vs `other.co.uk` are not.

`www.example.com` and `example.com` are one site and are always kept, whatever this is set to. Nearly every sitemap lists the apex, so a run that treated that pair as foreign would come back with nothing to check.

URLs on a genuinely different domain are always marked `cross_domain` and are never requested — a sitemap often lists CDN and partner hosts, and fetching them is not what you asked for.

proxyConfiguration.title: Proxy configuration
proxyConfiguration.description:
Optional proxy, for a stated geographic or access reason.

**This tool never rotates proxies.** If a target keeps answering `403` or serves a bot-challenge page, the run records it and moves on. Rotating proxies to get past a block is not something this product does — that is the line between checking status codes and evading a site's decision.

maxTotalChargeUsd.title: Max total charge (USD)
maxTotalChargeUsd.description:
Stop the run before it charges you more than this, in US dollars.

Rows are charged one pay-per-event item each. When the ceiling is reached, the run stops pushing rows and says so in the run summary (`rowsDroppedForChargeLimit`) — the dataset is cut, not lost. Leave empty to be governed only by the platform's own limit. This is a safety net, not a price quote: it bounds the charge, not the compute.

maxRequestsTotal.title: Max total requests
maxRequestsTotal.description:
The request budget for the whole run — sitemap fetches, redirect hops, retries and status probes all count against it. This is what stops a runaway run: one sitemap index can legally reference 50,000 child sitemaps, and the status check then doubles the request count.

When the budget runs out the run ends cleanly with `truncated: true` in the summary and the remaining URLs marked `skipped_budget`. It never fails silently.
